content.title: About
content.content: Unsweetened almond milk is a plant‑based beverage made by grinding almonds and straining the liquid. It has a light nutty note, a smooth creamy taste, and contains no added sugar.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Almond milk is a popular dairy‑free alternative for vegans and those with lactose intolerance.
It provides roughly 3‑4 times fewer calories than whole cow’s milk.
Unsweetened versions are often fortified with calcium, vitamin D and B12 to match the nutrient profile of dairy milk.
Production of almond milk uses less water than cow’s milk but more than soy milk.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Unsweetened almond milk typically contains 30‑40 kcal per 240 ml, making it suitable for weight management.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E is a powerful antioxidant that supports skin health and the immune system.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Almonds provide monounsaturated fats that may promote heart health.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Fortified versions deliver up to 30 % of the daily calcium requirement, important for bones and teeth.

items.title: Lactose‑free
items.content: Completely free of lactose, making it safe for people with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to almonds may experience reactions when consuming the product.

items.title: Low protein content
items.content: Compared with cow’s milk, almond milk provides little protein, so it should not be relied on as a primary protein source.

items.title: Additives and sweeteners
items.content: Some brands add flavorings or artificial sweeteners; choose a plain, additive‑free version if desired.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Almond milk works well with cereals, smoothies, coffee, baking, and sauces. Use it as a dairy substitute to add light texture and a subtle nutty flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store an opened carton in the refrigerator and consume within 5‑7 days. Unopened packages should be kept in a cool, dry place away from direct light.

content.title: About
content.content: Oil or table fat (NFS) is a food product derived from plant or animal fats, used in cooking for frying, baking, and dressing dishes. Depending on the source, the fat may be butter, sunflower, olive, rapeseed, etc. It is typically sold as a liquid oil or a solid fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The term NFS (Not For Sale) is often used in the food industry for products intended for internal use only.
Plant oils are rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids, while animal fats contain more monounsaturated and saturated fats.
Extra‑virgin olive oil is considered one of the healthiest oils due to its high oleic acid and polyphenol content.
Solid table fat (margarine) was first developed in the late 19th century as a butter substitute.
Some oils, such as flaxseed oil, require refrigeration to prevent oxidation.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Fats provide a concentrated source of calories (9 kcal/g), supplying quick energy reserves.

items.title: Supports vitamin absorption
items.content: Fat‑soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K are better absorbed when dietary fat is present.

items.title: Polyunsaturated fatty acids
items.content: Plant oils like sunflower and soybean contain omega‑6 and omega‑3 fatty acids important for heart and brain health.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Certain oils (e.g., olive oil) are rich in polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Excessive fat intake can lead to weight gain and increased risk of cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Solid fats and some plant oils high in saturated fatty acids may raise LDL‑cholesterol levels.

items.title: Oxidation and rancidity
items.content: Improper storage can cause oils to oxidize, forming harmful compounds.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, individuals may be sensitive to specific plant oils such as peanut oil.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Oil is suitable for frying, baking, making sauces, and dressing salads. Solid fat is often used in pastries to achieve a flaky texture. Before use, check the aroma—rancid smell indicates spoilage.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store oil in a tightly sealed container in a cool, dark place. Opened liquid plant oils last longer when kept in the refrigerator. Solid fat can be kept at room temperature, but for extended storage place it in the fridge. Discard the product if its color, smell, or taste changes.

content.title: About
content.content: Onion is a biennial herb from the Amaryllidaceae family. When cooked without added fat, onion retains its characteristic aroma and a sweetened flavor developed through heat. It is commonly used as a base ingredient in soups, sauces, stews, and side dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Onions contain sulfur compounds that form aromatic molecules when heated, giving cooked dishes their distinctive smell.
Heat reduces onion’s sharpness, turning it sweeter.
There are over 600 onion varieties differing in color, taste, and maturation time.
Onions are a staple in many culinary traditions, from French onion soup to Indian pakoras.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Onion provides quercetin and sulfur compounds that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Sulfur compounds can help lower cholesterol levels and improve vessel function.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity and participates in collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: May help regulate blood sugar
items.content: Phytochemicals in onion can improve insulin sensitivity.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to onion, such as skin itching or swelling.

items.title: Stomach irritation
items.content: People with sensitive stomachs may experience heartburn or discomfort after eating cooked onion.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Onion contains fructans, which can cause increased gas production in some people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked onion without added fat can be added to soups, stews, sauces, omelets, and vegetable casseroles. It also serves as an aromatic base for stocks. Sautéing in a dry pan or roasting in the oven preserves nutrients without extra oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh onions in a cool, dry, well‑ventilated place. Cooked onion should be kept in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Discard if it develops off‑odors or a slimy texture.

rice-white-with-tomatoes-and-or-tomato-b.title: White Rice with Tomatoes and/or Tomato‑Based Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: White rice is a polished grain product from which the husk and bran have been removed. In this version the rice is served with tomatoes and/or a tomato‑based sauce, adding bright flavor and a boost of vitamins and antioxidants.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rice is a staple food for more than half of the world’s population.
Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.
Tomato sauce is often made from ripe tomatoes, olive oil, and herbs, enhancing nutrient absorption.
White rice digests quickly, making it a common choice for recovery diets.
The rice‑and‑tomato combination is traditional in Mediterranean and Asian cuisines.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice provides complex carbohydrates, the body’s primary fuel for daily activities.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which support metabolism.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Tomatoes add dietary fiber and digestive enzymes that promote healthy gut function.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: May reduce cardiovascular risk
items.content: The blend of complex carbs from rice and potassium from tomatoes can help maintain healthy blood pressure.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice can cause a rapid rise in blood sugar, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes or tomato products.

items.title: Sodium in sauce
items.content: Prepared tomato sauce often contains added salt; choose low‑sodium versions when possible.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Tomatoes may be treated with pesticides; opting for organic or well‑washed produce reduces exposure.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the rice with tomatoes hot as a side dish or a main course. It pairs well with vegetables, meat, fresh herbs, a drizzle of olive oil, or a squeeze of lemon to brighten the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked rice with tomato sauce should be cooled promptly and stored in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days.
